name: The Gawain Romances
role: the code on trial in one man
one_line: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and the Loathly Lady who knows what women most desire — the chivalric code tested to destruction on a single knight.
apparatus:
The English poems put the whole apparatus of chivalry on one man and see what breaks.

***Sir Gawain and the Green Knight*** is the finest of them. A green giant rides into Camelot at Christmas and offers a game: strike me, and take my stroke in a year. Gawain strikes off his head; the giant picks it up and rides out. A year later, lodged with a host whose wife tests him for three mornings, Gawain does everything right except one thing — he accepts and conceals a green girdle he is told will keep him from being killed. *For what man soever is girded with this green lace, while he has it fastened neatly about him, there is no man under heaven who can cut him down.* One concealment, out of ordinary fear of death. The oath had nothing to say about it.

**The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnelle** inverts the whole question of sovereignty into comedy. Arthur must answer a riddle — what do women most desire — on pain of his life, and the answer, given by a loathly lady who demands Gawain in marriage as her price, is: *to have the sovereignty, without lying, of all, both high and low.* The right to rule moves from the throne to the marriage bed, and the poem thinks it is funny, and it is also entirely serious.
invented: The beheading game as a test of one conscience
The green girdle: the flaw no oath can legislate away
Sovereignty as the thing women want, asked as a riddle
inherited: Gawain from the French, where he had already begun to decline
bequeathed: An English Gawain who is the best of the court, against the French tradition that had demoted him
steelman: *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight* is the best poem in the Matter of Britain, and it locates the failure of chivalry exactly where the great cycles cannot: not in adultery or treason, but in a good man's ordinary wish not to die.
objection: These are small poems beside the cycles, and the surviving texts are hard — one manuscript for *Gawain*, blackletter scans for the rest. It is easy to over-read a body of work that survives so thinly.
how_it_maps: Carries the fellowship (the code tried on one knight) and the source of rule (Ragnelle's inversion). Reads against Malory, whose Gawain is a different and angrier man.
gap_note: Only *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight* is published here. The rest of the Madden volume — the Awntyrs, Golagros, the Carle of Carlisle — survives in an 1839 blackletter scan too rough to quote.
